title: Does reciprocity settle a disagreement?
subtitle: Two passages, different preferences, and the premises between them.
summary: Build a reasoned response to a disagreement over music and quiet. Separate the source words from assumptions you add, then test what changes when the roles reverse.
audience: Curious general readers; no specialist background required.
scope: Two English textual witnesses and an original hypothetical. This does not survey either tradition or establish historical influence.

passages.title: Reciprocity in an exchange
passages.text: What you do not want done to yourself, do not do to others.
passages.context: Tsze-kung asks for a rule to practise throughout life; the Master names reciprocity. These are Legge’s translated words in a transmitted dialogue, not an independently authenticated recording of a historical utterance.

passages.title: A directive in a teaching sequence
passages.text: Therefore, whatever you desire for men to do to you, you shall also do to them; for this is the law and the prophets.
passages.context: Verses 7–11 concern asking, seeking and knocking, parental bread/fish comparisons and the Father in heaven giving good things. Verse 12 follows with “Therefore”; the chapter closes by presenting Jesus as teacher. The exercise does not require religious assent.

claims.text: These English witnesses formulate reciprocity differently and belong to different textual settings.
claims.qualification: The comparison concerns these translations only; it establishes neither identical ethics nor influence.

claims.text: Applying either passage to the neighbor scenario requires interpretive and factual premises.
claims.qualification: The modern scenario and reconstructions below are original editorial examples, not claims that either source mentions them.

context: The selected Legge ebook labels the exchange XV.XXIII. The corresponding exchange is 15.24 in Eno’s 2015 English teaching translation, p.85. This resolves this pair of locators only; no reason for the discrepancy or universal modern numbering is asserted.
No Chinese or Greek original has been verified. Translation choices can affect this comparison.
The SEP discussion cautions that removing dialogue context can distort comparison. Neither short passage exhausts Confucian or Christian ethics.
A premise is a reason offered for a conclusion. An objection identifies a disputed premise or inference; it need not reject the whole source.

reviewLimitations: Local review covers source fidelity, evidence labeling and bounded prototype reuse. No professional specialist, screen-reader or learner session has been performed.

activity.scenario: Original hypothetical: one neighbor enjoys music while working; another needs quiet to concentrate. They share a wall. For this exercise these preferences are stipulated facts, not measured evidence. The available arrangements and their effects remain assumptions.
activity.definitions: Interpretation: a reading of the source. Empirical assumption: a testable claim about the situation. Normative addition: a claim about what people ought to do. Proposed conclusion: an action supported by the selected reasons; no automatic moral score is assigned.

premises.text: Ask whether imposing an unwanted interruption would be acceptable in the relevant reversed position.
Give the affected person’s actual need for concentration weight, rather than projecting the actor’s musical taste.
Headphones or another room are available and would reduce the disturbance without creating a comparable burden.
Read the directive as a reason to attend to how the other person would want to be treated in this setting.
Ask about the other person’s needs and seek terms both can reasonably accept.
A conversation and a workable quiet/music schedule are feasible here.

actions.label: Use headphones or move the music
actions.objection: This depends on a feasible alternative and a judgment about competing needs. The quoted words alone do not establish either.

actions.label: Ask and negotiate quiet/music times
actions.objection: Asking alone does not guarantee a fair agreement; a power imbalance or an essential need could remain.

actions.label: Continue playing music unchanged
actions.objection: Enjoying music yourself does not establish that the other person welcomes it. Explain why the affected person’s different preference can be set aside.

guides.title: An editorial reconstruction of restraint
guides.conclusion: On these added premises, choose a feasible arrangement that avoids imposing the unwanted interruption.
guides.objection: What counts as the relevant reversed position, and how competing needs should be weighed, remains contestable.

guides.title: An editorial reconstruction of responsive attention
guides.conclusion: On these added premises, ask about needs and negotiate an acceptable arrangement.
guides.objection: The actor can still project personal preferences, and consultation alone may leave unfair terms.

activity.transfer: Apply one reconstruction to a shared office where one person prefers a bright light and another is sensitive to glare. Identify what you would need to learn before recommending an action.
rubric: Identify the selected textual witness and its setting.
Label source wording, stipulated facts, interpretation, empirical assumptions and normative additions separately.
Explain a proposed action and an objection; swapping roles must not silently swap the other person’s preferences.
Allow another defensible reconstruction. Neither example belongs exclusively to one tradition.
